lead: The engine fuel system takes fuel from the tanks and meters the right flow to the combustor. The oil system pushes oil through the engine bearings and gears, removes their heat and carries wear debris to a filter and a chip detector. Every start, climb and cruise depends on both. Only a few universities teach this topic in detail, so keep the focus on the path, the jobs of the parts and the limits the crew watches.
prereq: You need: the engine control systems (FADEC) topic, for who commands the fuel flow.

blocks.text: Fuel is stored in wing, centre and sometimes tail tanks. Vents keep the tanks near outside pressure, and crossfeed valves let either engine draw from either side to keep the aircraft balanced. A boost pump in each tank pushes fuel to the engine at low pressure, so it does not boil or form vapour at altitude. On the engine, a low-pressure pump stage sends it through the fuel-oil heat exchanger, where hot oil warms the fuel (so ice crystals melt) and the fuel cools the oil, and then through the low-pressure fuel filter. The high-pressure pump, driven by the accessory gearbox, raises the pressure for metering. The fuel metering unit, commanded by the FADEC (full authority digital engine control), sets the flow for the thrust demanded: FADEC is the computer, the metering unit is the valve it drives. A flow meter reports the flow to the cockpit, and a high-pressure shut-off valve, worked by the start lever and the fire handle, isolates the nozzles. The start that follows is in engine starting and ignition.

blocks.where: ṁ is fuel mass flow in kg/s; ρ is density; V̇ is volume flow. With SI units, ρ in kg/m³ and V̇ in m³/s. With ρ in kg/L, V̇ must be in L/s.

items: The boost pump stops vapour lock; the HP pump makes metering pressure.
The filter bypass keeps fuel flowing if the filter blocks, and a pressure-drop switch warns the crew first.
The metering unit controls flow; it does not make pressure.

blocks.text: A jet engine usually has a dry-sump oil system: oil is kept in a separate tank, not in the engine. A pressure pump sends oil through a filter and cooler to bearings and gears. Oil takes heat from the bearings and carries metal particles. Scavenge pumps return oil from the bearing chambers to the tank. The filter has a bypass: if it blocks, unfiltered oil still reaches the bearings. A chip detector is a magnetic plug that catches steel particles and warns the crew. Oil pressure and temperature limits are in the flight manual.

blocks.where: Q is heat rate in kW; ṁ is oil mass flow in kg/s; c is specific heat in kJ/(kg·K); ΔT is oil temperature rise in K.

items: Wet sump stores oil in the engine sump; dry sump uses a tank and is common on jets.
The cooler may be the fuel-oil heat exchanger or a separate air-oil cooler.
A filter bypass warning means unfiltered oil is flowing.

examples.question: An engine burns 1200 kg/h of fuel of density 0.8 kg/L. Find the volume flow in L/s. Separately, 0.5 kg/s of oil with c = 2.0 kJ/(kg·K) picks up 60 kW from the bearings. Find the oil temperature rise, and the outlet temperature if the oil enters the bearings at 80 °C.
steps: Fuel volume flow = mass flow ÷ density = 1200 kg/h ÷ 0.8 kg/L = 1500 L/h.
Convert to seconds: 1500 L/h ÷ 3600 s/h = 0.4167 L/s, which rounds to 0.42 L/s.
Oil heat rate Q = 60 kW = 60 kJ/s.
examples.answer: Fuel volume flow is 0.42 L/s; the oil rises 60 K, from 80 °C to 140 °C.
examples.check:
mass=1200
density=0.8
vol_per_h=mass/density
vol_per_s=vol_per_h/3600
print(round(vol_per_s,2))
Q=60
m=0.5
c=2.0
dT=Q/(m*c)
print(dT)

traps: Boost pump and HP pump do different jobs; do not swap their pressures or purposes.
Filter bypass keeps oil flowing but sends unfiltered oil to bearings; it is not a clean-oil path.
The fuel-oil heat exchanger heats fuel and cools oil; oil temperature rise uses oil flow and oil specific heat.
kg/h to L/s needs density first; dividing by 3600 alone gives wrong units.

Mixing up the fuel shut-off valves: the HP shut-off valve at the engine is closed by the start lever; the fire handle also closes the low-pressure (spar) valve at the tank, so a nacelle fire is not fed from the tank.

quiz.q: What does the boost pump do?
quiz.a: It raises fuel pressure above vapour pressure at the tank, giving low-pressure feed and preventing vapour lock.

quiz.q: Why does the oil filter have a bypass?
quiz.a: If the filter blocks, the bypass opens so oil still reaches bearings; the oil is unfiltered, so a warning is serious.

quiz.q: Fuel flow is 900 kg/h, density 0.8 kg/L. Find L/s.
Oil flow falls but heat load stays fixed. What happens to ΔT and why?
quiz.a: ΔT = Q/(ṁc), so lower ṁ gives higher ΔT; the oil runs hotter.

quiz.q: Name two jobs of engine oil.
quiz.a: It removes heat from bearings and carries wear debris to the filter and chip detector; it also lubricates.

quiz.q: 0.4 kg/s oil, c = 2.0 kJ/(kg·K), picks up 40 kW. Find ΔT.
A fuel filter differential-pressure warning comes on in cruise. What has happened and what is the risk?
quiz.a: The filter is clogging (often with ice crystals or dirt), so the pressure drop across it is rising. If it blocks, the bypass opens and unfiltered fuel reaches the HP pump and metering unit, which can wear or jam. The fuel-oil heat exchanger is there to melt ice before the filter.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern engines use FADEC and health monitoring to watch fuel flow, oil pressure and chip signals. Airlines trend oil data to catch bearing wear before a failure. Newer work looks at electric pumps, sustainable aviation fuel effects on seals, and real-time debris sensors. Search "engine oil debris monitoring" and "FADEC fuel metering".
